title: Washington Moves to Hike H-1B Wage Floor by 30%
excerpt: A Trump DOL rule proposed March 27 would raise minimum H-1B salaries across all four tiers, with entry-level roles hit hardest.
body:
The U.S. Department of Labor dropped one of the most consequential immigration policy proposals in decades on March 27, 2026 — a draft rule that would raise the prevailing wage floor for H-1B, H-1B1, E-3, and PERM visa holders by an average of 30% across all four experience tiers.

**What the rule proposes:**
Entry-level (Level I) wages would rise to $97,746 — a hike of 33.39% — while Level II would reach $123,212 (up 24.47%), Level III $147,333 (up 20.79%), and Level IV $175,464 (up 21.68%). In a city like San Francisco, that means an entry-level software engineer would need to earn $162,000 annually to qualify — nearly 30% more than today.

**Why Washington is moving now:**
The rulemaking was directed by a September 2025 Presidential Proclamation, which declared that the H-1B program 'has been deliberately exploited to replace, rather than supplement, U.S. workers with lower-paid, lower-skilled labor.' DOL's own analysis found that the current methodology, in place since 2005, set prevailing wage tier levels too low — pegging Level I at just the 17th percentile of the wage distribution. Analyses by Lawfully and Threshold estimate the wage hike could cost major employers of foreign white-collar talent at least $18 billion in the first year, rising to $43 billion within three years as visas renew at higher rates.

**The broader squeeze on H-1B:**
This rule is part of a broader set of measures aimed at raising costs for H-1B employers — including a weighted H-1B lottery that now favors higher-wage workers, and the $100,000 fee imposed on certain H-1B petitions by the September 2025 Presidential Proclamation. If finalized, this rule would represent the most consequential change to prevailing wage methodology in more than two decades.

**What to watch:**
Similar wage hikes attempted in Trump's first term were blocked in court, but this proposal carries firmer legal footing — backed by a presidential proclamation — and remains open for public comment until May 26, 2026.

nri_angle: With Indians accounting for nearly 70% of H-1B approvals and tens of thousands of Indian-American tech workers on active H-1B status — many also mid-PERM green card process — this rule directly reshapes their job security, sponsorship prospects, and household finances.
